docs.title: About MeshCore Canada
docs.text:
MeshCore Canada is a community-run project for people using MeshCore in Canada. We maintain setup guides, community listings, Canadian region data, and links to shared tools.

MeshCore Canada is a volunteer community project and isn't affiliated with the official MeshCore project. For firmware, app, and protocol information, use the official MeshCore documentation.

docs.title: What the project maintains
docs.text:
• setup, hardware, and troubleshooting guides;
  • the Canadian community directory and the Find your zone page;
  • repeater and observer tools; and
  • the open-source website.

We also operate shared MQTT and Beacon services for Canadian users. Those services are maintained by Mr. Alderson, Ded, n30nex, and Kranic.

docs.title: The setup tool
docs.text:
The setup tool never asks for or stores your admin password or Wi-Fi password. Where a command needs one, it shows a placeholder for you to fill in yourself.

  • Sharing and resuming. The tool’s link (Copy a link to these answers, which is also the address in your browser) holds your non-secret answers, such as the repeater’s name, its region, the place you picked (a town, or a street address), and the coordinates of the pin you placed on the map, so you can share or resume a setup. It never holds passwords, Wi-Fi details, or a pasted region reply. Links can appear in browser history and server access logs, so don’t share one that holds a private location.
  • Map location. The tool shows a map with a pin, which you can move. The commands set your repeater’s location to the pin, and anyone can see that spot on public maps. Most people pick a spot a block or two from the repeater. If you tick Disable location, the tool leaves those commands out of the list, and the place and the pin stay out of the link too.
  • Switching language. So you don’t start over, the tool keeps your ticks, firmware version, and pasted replies in that browser tab, for the switch only. The other page uses them once, then removes them. If it doesn’t pick them up within 10 minutes, they’re ignored, and they go when you close the tab.
  • Region files. MeshMapper isn’t contacted unless you click a link to it. The setup tool, How repeaters work and Find your zone read region files published on this site.

docs.title: Saved on your device
docs.text:
The Find your zone page puts only the zone code and province you picked in its web address (URL), for example ?tag=ytr&province=on, so you can share or reload the page. It never puts a town, a street address, or coordinates there, and switching language carries nothing across. Links can appear in browser history and server access logs.

The retired region editor can download drafts saved in this browser. Downloading does not upload or delete them; old drafts are not approved MeshMapper boundaries.

Idea drafts and the last Beacon region code selected in the repeater-ID checker are saved in your browser only when you use those features. Repeater public keys, passwords, private keys, anti-spam tokens, and location searches are not saved there.

Aggregate header counts are cached for five minutes in the current browser tab. Community city searches appear in the page URL so you can share or revisit the results.

You can clear saved site data through your browser settings. The idea form also provides a Clear draft action.

docs.title: Observer data and privacy
docs.text:
Treat MeshCore radio traffic as public

MeshCore traffic is meant for shared mesh use, and networks may use different presets or frequencies. Treat every channel that uses a shared key, and private ones too, as insecure: any node on matching settings can be heard by observers on that mesh. Traffic forwarded over MQTT should be treated as public. Don't send names, locations, notes or other personal information you wouldn't want stored and shown publicly. Assume that even private channels could be collected and decrypted by someone with the means and know-how.

docs.title: What we collect
docs.text:
MeshCore Canada's MQTT brokers receive packet data from observers that capture MeshCore packets and forward telemetry.

Observers listen to all the MeshCore traffic they can hear on the settings they use. If an observer hears a packet and has packet publishing on, that packet can be sent to the MeshCore Canada brokers.

docs.title: Where data goes
docs.text:
Step What happens Radio traffic Nodes send MeshCore packets on the frequencies and settings of their local mesh. Observer capture Observers listen to all the traffic they can hear on their settings. MQTT publish Observers publish packet data to MeshCore Canada's brokers. Storage and display Data is stored on MeshCore Canada infrastructure and may be shown by Beacon and other public sites run by MeshCore Canada or approved operators.

No retention period has been published yet: don't assume data is deleted after a set time.

docs.title: Set up a network observer
docs.text: An observer forwards nearby MeshCore packet data to Beacon. It does not decrypt private messages or need to repeat traffic.

docs.title: How the pieces fit
docs.text:
1. Radiohears nearby MeshCore packets
  2. Observerforwards the packet data
  3. MeshCore Canadareceives it through two shared servers
  4. Live toolsBeacon shows observers and packets

The shared servers use MQTT, but you do not need to learn MQTT before choosing a setup.

Observers share what they hear

Observer details and heard packet data can appear in Beacon. Do not transmit sensitive information. Read Observer data and privacy before turning one on.

Your current setup Recommended method Host that must stay on RemoteTerm already manages the radio RemoteTerm The RemoteTerm host Home Assistant already has MeshCore Home Assistant Home Assistant PyMC already manages a repeater PyMC The PyMC host A Linux or macOS host is connected by USB MCtoMQTT The USB host A supported Wi-Fi LoRa board can be dedicated Repeater observer, set up in the guided tool No separate host

If none fit, ask in the MeshCore Canada forum before installing anything new.

docs.title: What every setup needs
docs.text:
Whichever setup you choose, you need:

  • a radio already set for the local mesh;
  • a real three-letter location code;
  • the MeshCore Canada primary and backup addresses;
  • encrypted connections with certificate checks;
  • packet publishing, not status-only publishing; and
  • an always-on host or board.

The Canadian onboarding baseline is Canada, 910.525 MHz / 62.5 kHz / SF7 / CR5, with 3-byte path hashes. A published local setting takes priority.

See the Canada preset and older-app guidance.

For exact broker fields, use the observer connection reference.

docs.title: Finish the check
docs.text:
Setup is not finished when a screen says “connected.” You are done when:

  1. your observer appears in Live observer list; and
  2. a packet heard by your radio appears in Live packets.

Finish with Check your observer. If something fails, go to Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Observer polling
docs.text:
Experimental

Polling runs on test firmware. Expect bugs, and don't put it on an observer you can't easily get to.

With polling on, an observer asks the repeaters right next to it for their battery, temperature and status, and sends the answers to Beacon (live.meshcore.ca) over the internet.

docs.title: Why it helps
docs.text:
Today, to check the battery on a far-away repeater, you log in from home. Your request is passed along by every repeater in between, and so is the answer. That keeps a lot of the mesh busy, and it often fails.

With polling, an observer that hears the repeater directly asks it for you. It takes one short radio exchange.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An observer with polling on registers with MeshCore Canada Beacon.
  2. Someone with a Beacon account asks to have their repeater polled, and gives its guest password.
  3. Beacon looks at the polling observers that hear that repeater directly (zero hops), picks the one with the strongest signal, and gives it the job.
  4. About once an hour, that observer asks the repeater for its battery, temperature and status, and uploads the answers to Beacon.

So if you run a polling observer, it may poll a zero-hop neighbour for someone else. If you run a repeater, you don't need a polling observer of your own: one nearby is enough.

  • Guest passwords only. A guest password can read stats and change nothing. Admin passwords are never accepted.
  • Direct neighbours only. The observer only talks to repeaters it hears directly (zero hops), so nothing is added to the rest of the mesh.
  • A light touch. At most two polls per repeater per hour, one at a time.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A board the polling firmware is built for. These are ESP32 boards with PSRAM (extra memory): Station G2, Station G3, Heltec V4 (including the expansion kit and R8 versions) and T-Beam S3 Supreme (SX1262). The Heltec V3 has no PSRAM, so it can't poll.
  • Wi-Fi where the observer sits.
  • Chrome or Edge on a computer, and a USB data cable.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
The first flash of the polling firmware needs Erase device, which wipes every setting on the board and its identity.

  • Write down its radio settings, name and admin password.
  • If the board is already in service, save its private key so it keeps its identity: send get prv.key and keep the reply in your password manager. Back up a running repeater has the steps.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
The setup tool does all of this for you. Pick Repeater observer, then ESP32 with PSRAM, then answer Yes when it asks about observer polling. It gives you the flashing steps and every command to paste.

To do it by hand:

  1. Open the observer flasher in Chrome or Edge.
  2. Choose MQTT Observer Firmware, your board, then Repeater.
  3. In Version, choose v1.18.0.1-poll. It isn't the newest in the list.
  4. The first time, tick Erase device. Later updates keep your settings.
  5. Flash it and wait for the board to restart.
  6. Set it up as a repeater observer: radio, name, Wi-Fi and the two MeshCore Canada servers. What each setting does lists those lines.

  7. Turn polling on:

    set poll.url https://live.meshcore.ca
set poll.requests on
set poll on

    set poll.requests on lets Beacon give your observer the repeaters that Beacon users ask to have polled.

Leave poll.slot and poll.consent alone. The observer finds the right MQTT slot by itself.

Beacon sets the minimum time between polls; set poll.interval (default 60 minutes) can only make it slower. It takes 30 to 1440 minutes.

To always poll a repeater of your own, whatever Beacon asks for, add it by its public key (64 characters). The observer has to hear it directly, and it holds up to 8:

poll add <repeater public key>

By default the observer tries a blank guest password, then hello. If a repeater uses another guest password, set it:

poll pw <repeater public key> set <guest password>

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
Command What you should see get poll Polling on, mode telemetry, an MQTT slot and the repeaters it polls get poll.status One line per repeater with its last result get poll.status 1 Details for the first repeater: battery, temperature, next poll poll now <repeater public key> One poll right away (at most one a minute) get mqtt.status Ends with poll: and how many repeaters answered

Readings show up on the repeater's page in Beacon, and the observer gets a Poller tag.

docs.title: If nothing happens
docs.text:
• get poll shows mode unknown: Beacon hasn't answered yet. Check poll.url and that Wi-Fi is up. Nothing is polled until the observer has set its clock over Wi-Fi.
  • No slot: no MQTT slot matches Beacon's servers. Check the MeshCore Canada servers in get mqtt.status.
  • not_direct: the observer hasn't heard that repeater directly in the last day.
  • login failed: the repeater doesn't accept a blank or hello guest login. Set its guest password with poll pw.
  • Polling stopped for one repeater: if a repeater lets the observer in as admin, the observer stops polling it and gives up that access. Fix the repeater's passwords, then send poll enable <repeater public key>.

More help: Troubleshoot an observer.

docs.title: Undo: go back to the regular firmware
docs.text:
Turn polling off with set poll off.

The polling firmware updates itself from the polling test channel. To go back to the regular observer firmware, send ota branch beta, then ota update.

docs.title: Observe with RemoteTerm
docs.text: RemoteTerm for MeshCore can forward packet data from a radio it already manages. It does not decrypt private messages.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
• RemoteTerm is installed from its reviewed upstream source.
  • The radio connection is stable.
  • The radio is on the local mesh settings.
  • You chose a real location code.
  • You read Observer data, access, and privacy.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
Open Settings → MQTT & Automation, add Community MQTT / meshcoretomqtt, and enter:

Field Primary value Name MeshCore.ca 1 Broker Host mqtt1.meshcore.ca Broker Port 443 Transport WebSockets Authentication Token WebSocket Path / Token Audience mqtt1.meshcore.ca Use TLS Enabled Verify TLS certificates Enabled Region Code The uppercase code from the Find your zone page Packet Topic Template meshcore/{IATA}/{PUBLIC_KEY}/packets

Leave optional owner email blank unless it is operationally needed. Save the entry as enabled.

Add a backup entry with the same values, changing only:

Field Backup value Name MeshCore.ca 2 Broker Host mqtt2.meshcore.ca Token Audience mqtt2.meshcore.ca

Use the same location code in both entries.

Windows MQTT fanout

If RemoteTerm's current upstream instructions require Uvicorn --loop none for Windows MQTT fanout, use that documented launch option. Confirm against the installed RemoteTerm version.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text: Your observer should show up within a few minutes in the Live observer list, with recent packets in Live packets. A connected status is not proof that packets arrived, so finish with Check your observer. Not showing? See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: Disable or remove only the two Community MQTT entries you added. Do not remove unrelated RemoteTerm automation. Confirm RemoteTerm still manages the radio normally.

docs.title: Troubleshoot an observer
docs.text: Start with what you can see. Change one part at a time so you know what fixed it.

docs.title: Observer never appears
docs.text:
Check these in order:

  1. Radio: confirm it is powered, connected to the observer method, and on the local mesh settings.
  2. Device or service: confirm the observer process is running.
  3. Broker: confirm that the observer reports a connection to the primary server with TLS verification.
  4. Viewer: wait a few minutes, refresh Live observer list, and search the exact observer name.

These commands only read service status:

MCtoMQTTCompanion capturePyMC 
sudo systemctl status mctomqtt --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u mctomqtt -n 80 --no-pager

sudo systemctl status meshcore-capture --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u meshcore-capture -n 80 --no-pager

sudo systemctl status pymc-repeater --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u pymc-repeater -n 80 --no-pager

Before sharing any output, follow What to share when asking for help.

For a repeater observer, run only these read commands in the device CLI:

get name
get wifi.status
get mqtt.iata
get mqtt.status
get mqtt1.preset
get mqtt2.preset
get path.hash.mode

You should see Wi-Fi and at least the primary broker connected, a three-letter location code, and the meshcore-ca-1 and meshcore-ca-2 presets.

docs.title: Observer appears but no packets arrive
docs.text:
A connected broker is not packet proof.

  1. Confirm the radio can hear normal nearby mesh activity.
  2. Confirm packet publishing is enabled for the selected method.
  3. Confirm the location code and packet topic agree.
  4. Check Live packets after nearby activity.
Method Packet setting Repeater observer get mqtt.packets is on, get bridge.enabled is on, and get mqtt.rx is on MCtoMQTT / companion capture Packet topic ends in /packets, not only /status PyMC Broker format is letsmesh Home Assistant Payload Mode is packet, or older Packets (Lets Mesh) is enabled RemoteTerm Community MQTT packet topic is enabled

If the radio hears nothing, resolve the radio preset, antenna, connection, or local activity before changing broker values.

docs.title: Only the backup connection fails
docs.text:
Compare the two entries. The backup host and token audience must both be mqtt2.meshcore.ca. A token for the primary host cannot authenticate to the backup.

Do not disable TLS verification to make the connection succeed.

docs.title: Observer appears in the wrong place
docs.text:
Check every configured location field. Use the same real three-letter location code in both broker entries and in the observer method.

Do not use:

  • CAN as shorthand for Canada;
  • XXX or HOME; or
  • a neighbouring code merely because an older picker does not list the correct code.

Update the integration if it cannot accept the correct code.

docs.title: Observer connects and disconnects repeatedly
docs.text:
Check in this order:

  1. stable power and USB connection;
  2. host sleep or service restarts;
  3. internet and DNS stability;
  4. system clock accuracy;
  5. repeated token, TLS, or WebSocket errors in local logs.

Record the time and time zone of one disconnect. That lets an administrator compare your report with infrastructure logs without exposing credentials.

docs.title: Home Assistant screen does not match the guide
docs.text:
Current screens use Payload Mode and a free-text location field. Older screens may use Packets (Lets Mesh) and a picker.

Update the integration before substituting a wrong location. If the current screen still differs, record the Home Assistant and MeshCore integration versions and ask for help.

  • unrelated lines from full config files.

Post it in the MeshCore Canada forum or your local community's support channel. Include only the small part of the log that shows the problem.

Return to Check your observer after each fix.

docs.title: Observe with MCtoMQTT
docs.text: MCtoMQTT reads packets from a USB-connected MeshCore radio and publishes them from an always-on Linux or macOS host.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
Requirement Check Radio Packet logging works over USB and the local mesh settings are correct Host Linux or macOS for meshcoretomqtt; Windows is supported only for companion capture Access You can read the current config and restart the service Location A real three-letter location code Tools curl, a text viewer, and systemctl on Linux

Review before running

These helpers are not pinned to a release or checksum. Download and inspect them before running. --no-restart still writes files; it is not a dry run.

Files to review:

  • Bash helper source
  • Published Bash helper
  • PowerShell companion helper source

docs.title: What this changes
docs.text:
On a serial host, the helper:

  • writes /etc/mctomqtt/config.d/20-meshcore-ca.toml;
  • makes a timestamped .bak.<timestamp> copy when that file exists;
  • adds the primary and backup MeshCore Canada addresses and location code; and
  • restarts mctomqtt unless --no-restart is used.

For companion capture, it updates ~/.meshcore-packet-capture/.env.local, makes a timestamped backup, updates existing Canada broker slots or uses empty slots, and may restart the capture service.

Install flags download and run separate upstream installers. Do not use them until you have reviewed the named upstream installer too.

docs.title: 1. Download and inspect the helper
docs.text:
workdir="$(mktemp -d)"
curl -fsSLo "$workdir/add-meshcore-ca-broker.sh" https://meshcore.ca/analyzer/scripts/add-meshcore-ca-broker.sh
less "$workdir/add-meshcore-ca-broker.sh"

Check the source URL, changed paths, server addresses, backup behaviour, and restart behaviour. Keep the file for the rest of this setup.

docs.title: 2. Write without restarting
docs.text:
Replace YOW with your code from the Find your zone page:

bash "$workdir/add-meshcore-ca-broker.sh" --device serial-host --iata YOW --no-restart

The helper validates the code shape, rejects XXX, warns on codes outside its quick list, and prints the changed and backup paths.

docs.title: 3. Review the result
docs.text:
sudo sed -n '1,220p' /etc/mctomqtt/config.d/20-meshcore-ca.toml

Check that:

  • the location code is correct;
  • primary host and audience are mqtt1.meshcore.ca;
  • backup host and audience are mqtt2.meshcore.ca;
  • port is 443, transport is WebSockets, and TLS verification is enabled.

Do not paste the full file into a public issue without reviewing it.

docs.title: 4. Restart deliberately
docs.text:
sudo systemctl restart mctomqtt
sudo systemctl status mctomqtt --no-pager

The service should stay active without repeated TLS or authentication errors.

docs.title: Run it directly after review
docs.text:
After reviewing the current published helper, you can run that same file directly:

bash add-meshcore-ca-broker.sh --device serial-host --iata YOW

The downloaded-file method above is easier to review and recover.

docs.title: Fresh installation
docs.text:
--install-mctomqtt downloads and runs the upstream meshcoretomqtt installer. Review that installer first, then add the flag:

bash "$workdir/add-meshcore-ca-broker.sh" --device serial-host --iata YOW --install-mctomqtt

The upstream installer controls serial-port selection and package changes, and it is not pinned or checksummed here.

docs.title: Companion capture
docs.text:
Set the companion radio to the local mesh settings first.

Linux or macOSWindows PowerShell

Review the same Bash helper, then run:

bash "$workdir/add-meshcore-ca-broker.sh" --device companion --iata YOW --no-restart

Review ~/.meshcore-packet-capture/.env.local, then restart your capture process.

Download and inspect the helper before running:

$helper = Join-Path $env:TEMP "add-meshcore-ca-packetcapture-broker.ps1"
Invoke-WebRequest https://meshcore.ca/analyzer/scripts/add-meshcore-ca-packetcapture-broker.ps1 -OutFile $helper
Get-Content $helper
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $helper -Iata YOW

The PowerShell helper changes %USERPROFILE%\.meshcore-packet-capture\.env.local and creates a backup. Its optional install switch executes an upstream installer and must be reviewed first.

There is no documented meshcoretomqtt Windows installer for the packet-log serial-host path.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text: Your observer should show up within a few minutes in the Live observer list, with recent packets in Live packets. A connected status is not proof that packets arrived, so finish with Check your observer. Not showing? See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
Use the exact backup path printed by the helper.

If a serial-host drop-in existed before:

sudo cp -- '/etc/mctomqtt/config.d/20-meshcore-ca.toml.bak.<timestamp>' '/etc/mctomqtt/config.d/20-meshcore-ca.toml'
sudo systemctl restart mctomqtt

If the helper created a new drop-in and no prior file existed:

sudo rm -- '/etc/mctomqtt/config.d/20-meshcore-ca.toml'
sudo systemctl restart mctomqtt

For companion capture, restore the printed .env.local.bak.<timestamp> over .env.local, preserve its permissions, and restart the capture process.

The helper does not uninstall software added by an upstream install flag. Use that upstream project's reviewed uninstall process.

docs.title: Observe with Home Assistant
docs.text: Use the MeshCore integration you already run in Home Assistant to publish packet telemetry to MeshCore Canada.

docs.title: Check your screen
docs.text:
Current MeshCore integrations use these fields:

Packet control Location control Payload Mode = packet Free-text Broker IATA Code

If your screen looks different, see Home Assistant screen does not match the guide. Update the integration if it cannot accept the correct location code; do not substitute a nearby code.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
• Home Assistant and the MeshCore integration are healthy.
  • The radio is connected over a supported USB, BLE, or TCP path.
  • The radio uses the local mesh settings.
  • You chose a real location code.
  • You read Observer data, access, and privacy.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
Open:

Settings → Devices & Services → MeshCore → Configure → Manage MQTT Brokers

Add the primary entry:

Field Value Server mqtt1.meshcore.ca Port 443 Transport websockets Use TLS Enabled TLS Verify Enabled Username / Password Leave blank Use MeshCore Auth Token Enabled Token Audience mqtt1.meshcore.ca Payload Mode packet Status Topic meshcore/{IATA}/{PUBLIC_KEY}/status Packets Topic meshcore/{IATA}/{PUBLIC_KEY}/packets

Set the integration's location field to the uppercase code from the Find your zone page.

Add the backup entry with the same settings, changing only:

Field Value Server mqtt2.meshcore.ca Token Audience mqtt2.meshcore.ca

Leave optional owner fields blank unless they are needed. Save both entries.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text: Your observer should show up within a few minutes in the Live observer list, with recent packets in Live packets. A connected status is not proof that packets arrived, so finish with Check your observer. Not showing? See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: Disable or remove only the two MeshCore Canada broker entries you added. Keep unrelated Home Assistant integrations and the radio connection unchanged. Confirm the original MeshCore integration still operates.

docs.title: Observe with PyMC
docs.text: Add MeshCore Canada's primary and backup addresses to your PyMC repeater service.

docs.title: Check your installation
docs.text: This procedure is for a Linux systemd service named pymc-repeater with config at /etc/pymc_repeater/config.yaml. Confirm the version, service name, path, and config format before editing. For different paths, macOS, or Windows, follow the installed PyMC version's documentation.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
• PyMC is healthy before the change.
  • You know the actual service and config paths.
  • The radio uses the local mesh settings.
  • You chose a real location code.
  • You can restore a root-owned backup.

Record the current service state:

sudo systemctl status pymc-repeater --no-pager
backup="/etc/pymc_repeater/config.yaml.pre-meshcore-ca.$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%S).$"
sudo cp --no-clobber -- /etc/pymc_repeater/config.yaml "$backup"
printf 'Backup: %s\n' "$backup"

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
In /etc/pymc_repeater/config.yaml, set the location code inside mqtt:

mqtt:
  iata_code: YOW

Replace YOW with your code from the Find your zone page.

Under mqtt.brokers, add:

- name: MeshCore-CA
  enabled: true
  host: mqtt1.meshcore.ca
  port: 443
  transport: websockets
  format: letsmesh
  disallowed_packet_types: []
  retain_status: false
  tls:
    enabled: true
    insecure: false
  use_jwt_auth: true
  audience: mqtt1.meshcore.ca
- name: MeshCore-CA Backup
  enabled: true
  host: mqtt2.meshcore.ca
  port: 443
  transport: websockets
  format: letsmesh
  disallowed_packet_types: []
  retain_status: false
  tls:
    enabled: true
    insecure: false
  use_jwt_auth: true
  audience: mqtt2.meshcore.ca

Do not add an MQTT password. Leave optional owner email blank unless it is operationally needed.

Review the edited section, then restart:

sudo systemctl restart pymc-repeater
sudo systemctl status pymc-repeater --no-pager

If the service fails, inspect a short local excerpt:

sudo journalctl -u pymc-repeater -n 80 --no-pager

Review any output before sharing it. Follow the redaction checklist.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text: Your observer should show up within a few minutes in the Live observer list, with recent packets in Live packets. A connected status is not proof that packets arrived, so finish with Check your observer. Not showing? See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
Restore the exact backup made before editing:

sudo cp -- "${backup:?Set backup to the saved backup path first}" /etc/pymc_repeater/config.yaml
sudo systemctl restart pymc-repeater
sudo systemctl status pymc-repeater --no-pager

Keep the failed file privately if it helps with diagnosis. Do not post it without removing secrets and personal details.

docs.title: Set up a repeater
docs.text:
Answer a few questions, one at a time, and get every command to paste into your repeater, with what each one does.

Before you start: pick a supported board, agree on the site with your local community, and set it up on the bench before it goes up the mast.

The setup tool didn't load. Reload the page.

The setup tool needs JavaScript. [How repeaters work](guide.md) explains every step and command it would show.

docs.title: After it's set up
docs.text:
• Check that a nearby companion hears its advert. Each time it reboots, set its clock again with clock sync from the MeshCore app. After a restart its clock is often wrong, and phones may ignore its announcements until it's set.
  • Choose an antenna and a mount.
  • On firmware 1.14 or newer, read about loop detection before changing a community repeater.
  • Something not working? Get help.

Region data: sources and licences

docs.title: How repeaters work
docs.text:
This page explains the ideas behind the setup tool: what a repeater does, how scopes and regions decide where messages go, and what each command in the tool's list means. You don't need to read it first: the tool asks one question at a time and explains every command as you go.

On this page: What a repeater is · Repeater observers · Scopes and regions · What each setting does · City or edge repeater · Companion scopes · Starter regions

docs.title: What a repeater is
docs.text:
A repeater passes messages on so they reach further.

It's a MeshCore radio that stays switched on in one place, ideally up high on a roof or a mast. Nobody chats on it. People chat on a companion: the small radio they pair with the MeshCore app on their phone or computer. When a repeater hears a message, it can send it out again, so it reaches people who are too far away to hear the companion. Each repeater that passes a message on is one hop.

Before it passes a message on, a repeater checks two things:

  • Is the message labelled for somewhere it serves? Its region list decides that. See Scopes and regions.
  • Has it gone too far already? After 16 hops, no repeater passes it on.

Every device nearby has to use the same radio settings, or they can't hear each other. Most of Canada uses the Canada radio settings; some local groups use their own.

To set one up, use the setup tool. For hardware and where to put it, see repeater devices and mounting options.

docs.title: What a repeater observer is
docs.text:
A repeater observer is a repeater that also reports what it hears to live.meshcore.ca, so everyone can see how the mesh is doing. It needs Wi-Fi to do that.

That's why it needs an ESP32 board: nRF52 boards have no Wi-Fi. It runs the observer firmware from the observer flasher, under MQTT Observer Firmware. Its reports go over your Wi-Fi to the two MeshCore Canada servers, using MQTT (a common way for devices to send reports to a server).

It works in one of two ways:

  • Repeat and observe: a full repeater that also reports what it hears. Most people pick this.
  • Listen only: it reports what it hears to live.meshcore.ca but never passes anything on.

On an ESP32 board with PSRAM (extra memory), such as a Station G2, Station G3, Heltec V4 or T-Beam S3 Supreme, it can also ask nearby repeaters for their battery and status. That's observer polling, which is experimental.

Either way it reports what it hears. Listen only is handy indoors or next to another repeater, where repeating would only add noise. You can switch later with set repeat on or set repeat off.

A repeater observer is one kind of observer. Others use RemoteTerm, Home Assistant or a small computer next to a radio: Set up a network observer helps you choose one. Observer data and privacy explains what the reports contain.

docs.title: Scopes and regions
docs.text:
A scope is a label on a message saying how far it should travel. A region list is the labels a repeater agrees to pass on.

That's the whole idea. For example:

  • A message labelled ytr stays around Belleville. Repeaters in Quinte West have ytr on their list, so they pass it on. Kingston's repeaters don't, so it stops there.
  • A message labelled on crosses Ontario, because every Ontario repeater has on on its list.

docs.title: One code, two names
docs.text:
The same short codes show up in two places:

  • On a message, the label is a scope. You set it on your companion and on each channel. The MeshCore app calls it a region scope.
  • On a repeater, the labels it passes on are its regions, kept in its region list.

A region is also the area a repeater serves. Regions are named after the nearest airport code: Belleville is in ytr, Quinte West. A repeater's region decides which messages it passes on.

docs.title: Which region is mine?
docs.text:
The setup tool finds it from the town, street address or coordinates where the repeater will be, and the Find your zone page shows them all. Coordinates aren't sent to any search; a town or street address is looked up with the Government of Canada's place search (geo.ca).

  • Near a provincial border, pick the side it's really on. The yow region crosses the Ottawa River: an Ottawa repeater has yow and on, a Gatineau repeater yow and qc. A street address or coordinates settle it.
  • Towns in the same region share its code. Ottawa and Gatineau are both yow.
  • No zone for your area? MeshMapper, the community map that draws each region's area, doesn't cover everywhere. The Find your zone page then shows a MeshCore Canada starter region instead.
  • Write codes in lowercase. You can search for YTR, but on the air ytr and YTR are two different labels.

docs.title: The five labels
docs.text:
From smallest to largest:

Label Example What it covers Region ytr, yow, yhz One area, named after its airport code Province or territory on, qc, ns The province the repeater is in Ontario + Québec onqc Both provinces, as one shared mesh Canada can All of Canada. On every list, not used yet North America na Canada and the US. On every list, not used yet

A Belleville repeater has ytr, on, onqc, can and na. A Halifax repeater has yhz, ns, can and na: onqc is only for Ontario and Québec.

can and na are on every list so that Canada-wide or cross-border messages can work one day without anyone setting up their repeater again. Don't use them on your companion or channels yet: on their own, they don't make a message reach another province or country.

Each label stands alone. The labels go from small to large, but they don't sit inside each other: having on doesn't mean having ytr. Each label has to be on the list by itself, which is why the setup tool puts every one that applies on every repeater.

docs.title: How a repeater decides
docs.text:
When a message reaches a repeater, the repeater compares its label with its list:

  • The label is on its list: it passes the message on.
  • The label isn't on its list: it doesn't.
  • No label at all: the message counts as *, the star that stands for "no label". It's passed on only if * is allowed, which city repeaters do and edge repeaters don't. Older apps send messages with no label, and so does a companion with no default scope.
  • Too many hops: after 16 hops it stops, whatever its label.

A Belleville city repeater's list is *, ytr, on, onqc, can and na. So:

Message Label Belleville city repeater Belleville test channel ytr Passes it on First message to a friend in Montréal onqc Passes it on Someone on an older app none Passes it on Kingston channel ygk Doesn't pass it on Québec-wide channel qc Doesn't pass it on

The repeater still hears every message: its list only decides which ones it passes on. Your companion receives everything that reaches it.

A few details catch people out:

  • Spelling must be exact. ytr, YTR and quinte are three different labels.
  • Only messages that spread out are checked. Channel messages, and the first direct message to a contact, spread out through every repeater that will pass them on. This is called a flood. Once a direct message has a known path, it follows that path and labels no longer matter.
  • A repeater with no regions set passes on only messages with no label. A labelled message only travels once the repeaters along the way have its label.
  • A label isn't a lock or a fence. Anyone can put any label on a message, and it doesn't check where you are. It only tells repeaters whether to pass the message on.

docs.title: Who passes on what
docs.text:
Here's a stretch of mesh from Belleville to Kingston, with an edge repeater in between:

  • Belleville city repeaters have *, ytr, on, onqc, can and na.
  • The edge repeater has ytr, ygk, on, onqc, can and na, but not *.
  • Kingston city repeaters have *, ygk, on, onqc, can and na.

Does each repeater pass the message on?

  • No label, sent in Belleville: Belleville passes it on. The edge repeater doesn't, so Kingston isn't reached. It stays around Belleville.
  • ytr, a Belleville channel: Belleville and the edge repeater pass it on. Kingston's repeaters don't, so it stops there.
  • ygk, a Kingston channel: the edge repeater and Kingston pass it on. Belleville doesn't, so it stays around Kingston.
  • on, an Ontario channel: all three pass it on, so it goes across Ontario.
  • onqc, a companion's default: all three pass it on, so it goes across Ontario and Québec.

This shows which repeaters pass a message on, not radio coverage. Anyone in range of a repeater still hears what it sends, and real meshes have more paths than this.

docs.title: Try it: which towns does a label reach?
docs.text:
This example shows which towns' city repeaters pass on a message, for each label you could put on it.

The example needs JavaScript to run. The table and list above show the same idea.

docs.title: Why airport codes?
docs.text:
• MeshMapper already uses them, for example ytr.meshmapper.net.
  • MeshCore already uses them elsewhere, such as the location code every observer reports. A second set of names just for regions would only add confusion.
  • There are no accents or capital letters to get wrong. montréal, Montreal and montreal would be three different labels.
  • They're easy to split later. If a town wants its own area one day, it can use its own airport code and still keep its province and onqc.

The code names the area, not the airport. The codes come from IATA, the airline industry group that assigns airport codes, which is why they are called IATA codes.

docs.title: Reading a region def line
docs.text:
You don't need this to set up a repeater: the tool gives you the exact line. It helps when you want to read one.

region def ytr|* on|* onqc|* can|* na

region def builds the repeater's list in one line. It adds each name in turn, and |* means "go back to the top" before the next one, so the names end up side by side, not inside each other. Send region afterwards to see the list:

*^ F
 ytr F
 on F
 onqc F
 can F
 na F
  • F means it passes those messages on.
  • The * line is for messages with no label. It has F on a city repeater and no F on an edge repeater.
  • ^ marks its home region. On a new repeater it sits on *. You can ignore it.

region def only adds names. It never removes the ones already there, so a repeater that's already running has its old regions cleared first: see Clearing old regions. Firmware older than 1.16 builds the same list one name per line: see Older firmware.

docs.title: How messages find their way between cities
docs.text:
You don't need to hear every repeater along the way to message someone in another city. The first direct message to a contact, before a path is known, spreads out through the mesh with your default scope. The reply that tells your companion the path comes back with your contact's default scope. After that, messages follow the saved path and labels no longer matter.

So both default scopes have to be labels the repeaters in between pass on. Repeaters set up with the tool in Ontario and Québec all have onqc, so it works between Belleville and Montréal in both directions. A region label like ytr stops at the first repeater without it, just outside Quinte West, and a message with no label stops at the first edge repeater. That's why companions set a default scope: see Companion scopes.

You still need your contact's details and working radio links between you. The MeshCore FAQ explains how paths are found.

docs.title: What each setting does
docs.text:
The setup tool explains every command in its list in one sentence. These are the same explanations, all in one place. The examples are for a repeater in Belleville, whose region is ytr (Quinte West). Your list uses your own town, region and name.

You paste the commands one at a time into the flasher's Console, or send them from the repeater's Command Line in the MeshCore app. Most answer OK. Lines with words between < and > are ones you type yourself: the tool never asks for your passwords, so it can't copy them for you.

docs.title: Basics
docs.text:
set radio 910.525,62.5,7,5 Use the Canada radio settings: 910.525 MHz, 62.5 kHz, spreading factor 7, coding rate 5. Every device nearby has to match. set radio 910.425,62.5,7,5

Use the BC Mesh radio settings: 910.425 MHz, 62.5 kHz, spreading factor 7, coding rate 5. Every device nearby has to match.

The tool asks which settings to use only where a local group, such as BC Mesh in British Columbia, uses its own.

When you send the commands from your phone, the radio line is left out: changing the radio settings from your phone would cut off the connection you're using.

set name Belleville_R1

The name other people see.

Keep it to about 30 letters (accented letters count as two). Spaces are fine, but not [ ] \ : , ? *: the repeater won't accept them.

set lat 44.1628 Show it on maps at the spot you picked. This line sets the latitude. set lon -77.3832

This line sets the longitude, so maps show it at the spot you picked.

The tool shows a map with a pin where you said it will be installed. Drag it, tap the map, or type the coordinates. Most people pick a spot a block or two from the repeater. Tick Disable location and both lines are left out, so maps won't show it.

password <your new admin password> Set the admin password you'll use to manage it from the app. Keep it in your password manager. password <your new admin password>, on a repeater that's already running Change the admin password, or skip this line to keep the current one. Keep it in your password manager.

docs.title: MeshCore Canada settings
docs.text:
The tool gives these four to every repeater, so repeaters across the mesh behave the same way. An announcement (advert) is how a device tells others it exists. These save by themselves.

set path.hash.mode 2 Use longer repeater IDs (3 bytes) in the list of repeaters a message went through, so fewer repeaters share an ID. set advert.interval 240 Announce itself to repeaters in direct range every 4 hours. set flood.advert.interval 47 Announce itself across the wider mesh every 47 hours. set flood.max 16 Never pass on a message after 16 hops (each repeater that passes it on is one hop).

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
The scope lines for a Belleville city repeater on firmware 1.16 or newer:

region def ytr|* on|* onqc|* can|* na Pass on messages labelled for Quinte West (ytr), Ontario (on), Ontario + Québec (onqc), Canada (can) and North America (na). region allowf * Also pass on messages with no label, as a city repeater does. region denyf *

Don't pass on messages with no label, so they stay in their own region. That's what makes it an edge repeater.

An edge repeater gets this line instead of region allowf *.

region default ytr Label this repeater's own announcements with ytr. region save Save the region settings.

docs.title: Back up a running repeater
docs.text:
A repeater that's already running has an identity: its private key. Other devices know it by that key, and it can't be recreated if it's lost. Before you flash it, back it up:

  1. Write down its name and admin password.
  2. To save its private key, in the MeshCore app open the repeater from Contacts, log in as admin, tap Command Line and send get prv.key. Or connect it by USB, open the Console in the MeshCore flasher and send the same command. Keep the reply in your password manager and never paste it anywhere shared.
  3. Never erase it in the flasher.

If flashing wipes it anyway, for example when you switch to the observer firmware, put the key back. Right after flashing, while it's still plugged in, send set prv.key <saved key> in the flasher's Console, then reboot. Put the key you saved in place of <saved key>. You can also do it later from the app's Command Line if you can log in as admin; if you can't, plug it in by USB and use the flasher's Console. Both commands are in the MeshCore command reference.

Never share the private key: anyone who has it can pose as your repeater.

docs.title: Clearing old regions
docs.text:
A repeater that's already running may still have regions from an older setup. region def doesn't remove them, so the tool's list clears them first.

region Show the regions it has now. Paste the reply into the setup tool to clear the old ones. region remove ott Remove the old region ott. region home ytr

Make ytr its home region, since its old home region is being removed.

This line only appears when the ^ home marker was on one of the old regions.

The tool removes the most indented names first and never removes *. If region remove answers Err - not empty, another name is still indented under it: remove that one first, then try again. Err - not found means it's already gone, which is fine.

From the app, a long reply can be cut short. If the list looks cut off, or the repeater has many regions, run region over USB instead, in the flasher's Console.

docs.title: Older firmware
docs.text:
Firmware 1.16 and newer builds the whole list with one region def line. Older versions add one name per line, so these lines repeat for each label.

Firmware 1.15:

region put ytr Pass on messages labelled for Quinte West (ytr).

Firmware 1.14:

region put ytr Add Quinte West (ytr) to its list of regions. It doesn't pass those messages on until its region allowf line. region allowf ytr Pass on messages labelled for Quinte West (ytr).

Firmware 1.14 has no region default, so the repeater's own announcements carry no label. Updating is worth it. Below 1.14, region settings don't work: update the firmware first.

docs.title: Repeater observer
docs.text:
These lines are only for a repeater observer.

set mqtt.iata YTR

Tell live.meshcore.ca which region it reports from.

It's the region code, in capitals.

set wifi.powersave none Keep Wi-Fi awake so reports aren't delayed. set mqtt1.preset meshcore-ca-1 Report to the main MeshCore Canada server. This replaces whatever is in MQTT slot 1, the first of its saved server connections. set mqtt2.preset meshcore-ca-2

Report to the backup MeshCore Canada server too. This replaces whatever is in MQTT slot 2, the second of its saved server connections.

If this board already reports to another network in those slots, use the observer flasher's Configure via USB to put MeshCore Canada in free slots (3 to 6) instead.

set mqtt.status on Send a short status report when it connects and every few minutes, so live.meshcore.ca shows it as online. set mqtt.packets on Report the packets (radio messages) it hears. This is the main thing it sends to the servers. set mqtt.raw off Don't also send a raw copy of each packet. The servers don't need it. set mqtt.rx on Include the packets it receives over the radio. set mqtt.tx advert Of the packets it sends itself, report only its own announcements. set bridge.enabled on Turn on sending over Wi-Fi. This is the main switch for everything it reports. set repeat on Also pass messages on, as a full repeater. set repeat off Listen only: never pass messages on. advert Announce itself now, so nearby devices see it straight away. set wifi.ssid <your Wi-Fi name> Your 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network. Type its name exactly, without quotes. set wifi.pwd <your Wi-Fi password> Your Wi-Fi password. Never paste this anywhere shared.

docs.title: Observer polling
docs.text:
These lines are only for a repeater observer with polling turned on. Polling is experimental and needs its own test firmware: Observer polling explains it.

set poll.url https://live.meshcore.ca Send its readings to Beacon, at live.meshcore.ca. set poll.requests on Let Beacon give it the repeaters that Beacon users ask to have polled. set poll on Turn polling on.

docs.title: Finish
docs.text:
reboot Restart so every setting takes effect.

After it restarts, the tool lists a few checks, such as ver and region. They only show its settings. The one exception is clock sync, which sets its clock from your phone: after a restart its clock is often wrong, and phones may ignore its announcements until it's set. Send it from the MeshCore app. It doesn't work from the Console: there the repeater only answers that its clock can't go backwards.

docs.title: Loop detection
docs.text: The tool doesn't change this setting. Firmware 1.14 and newer can drop packets that keep coming back through the same repeater, which can calm a flood of repeated packets. Change it only with your local operators: write down the current value with get loop.detect, set it with, for example, set loop.detect moderate, and put the old value back if messages start going missing. See the MeshCore command reference.

docs.title: City or edge repeater
docs.text:
Edge repeaters regularly hear repeaters in another region, for example one between Belleville and Kingston. City is every other repeater, even on the outskirts. Edge repeaters stop messages with no label from spilling into the next region.

The difference is what they do with messages that have no label:

  • A city repeater passes them on (region allowf *), so people nearby who haven't set a scope are still heard.
  • An edge repeater doesn't (region denyf *). It also has the codes of the neighbouring regions it hears, so labelled messages for either side get through.

Belleville, city repeater:

region def ytr|* on|* onqc|* can|* na
region allowf *
region default ytr

Belleville, edge repeater that also hears Kingston (ygk):

region def ytr|* ygk|* on|* onqc|* can|* na
region denyf *
region default ytr

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Without edge repeaters, every message with no label would spread from town to town across the whole mesh, crowding the radio channel everywhere. Edge repeaters keep that local chatter in its own region, while labelled messages still travel as far as their label says.

docs.title: Is mine an edge repeater?
docs.text:
• Being near a boundary isn't enough. What counts is which repeaters it regularly hears.
  • Check its neighbours on MeshMapper. Click your repeater to see the repeaters it hears, with how often and how recently each link was seen. Several neighbours in another region, heard often and recently, make it an edge repeater. A single link seen a few times, or not for weeks, doesn't count.
  • Towns that share a code are one region. Ottawa and Gatineau are both yow, so a repeater between them is a city repeater.
  • Think twice if it's the only repeater around. An edge repeater doesn't pass on messages from people nearby who haven't set a scope.
  • Every repeater linking the same two regions should be an edge repeater. Otherwise messages with no label go around through the one that isn't.

An edge repeater lists the neighbouring regions it regularly hears. It will also carry messages labelled for these. They're optional: without them, it still passes on on, onqc and the other wider labels. The tool lists the five regions nearest to your repeater first, with how far each is, and has a box to find any other region.

docs.title: Labels shared across the border
docs.text:
Some repeaters link with a network in the United States. For those, the tool offers agreed scopes: labels that operators on both sides have agreed to carry. It shows the ones that suit your province, each with a short description. City and edge repeaters can both use them. For example, onny is for repeaters that connect Ontario and New York.

You can also tick Another scope we've agreed with a network across the border, for any repeater in any province. Type the scope name exactly as you both agreed it (lowercase letters, numbers and dashes).

Only tick one if this repeater links with that network and its operators have agreed. Not sure? Leave them off.

Using a cross-border scope that isn't listed? Share it with us so it can be added to the tool.

docs.title: Still too noisy?
docs.text: If messages with no label are still too noisy inside a region, repeaters can also limit how far they travel with set flood.max.unscoped 3. Labelled messages keep the 16-hop limit. The tool doesn't add this line: only use it if your local operators agree.

docs.title: Companion scopes
docs.text:
Your companion puts a scope on what you send. Each channel can have its own, and everything else uses your default scope.

Set your default scope now

Repeaters set up with the meshcore.ca setup tool pass messages on by scope. Edge repeaters don't pass on messages that have no scope, so without a default scope your messages may not reach beyond your own area.

  • Ontario or Québec: use onqc.
  • Elsewhere: use your province's code, such as ns or bc, unless your community has agreed on something else.

In the MeshCore app, version 1.43 or newer, it's under Settings → Network Settings → Default Region Scope. The companion guide shows each step with screenshots.

Why onqc? You can't give a single direct message its own scope. The first one to a contact uses your default scope, and the reply that sets up the path uses your contact's (see How messages find their way between cities). onqc is passed on across both provinces, so it works between any two cities there. Elsewhere there's no label shared between provinces, so your province's code is the widest one in use. Don't use can or na yet.

docs.title: Scope a channel
docs.text:
A channel with no scope of its own uses your default scope. To give a channel its own, pick its label from this table, then follow the steps below.

Channel Scope Public onqc in Ontario and Québec; your province's code elsewhere Test channels, such as #testing Your region, such as ytr Bot channels, such as #bots Your region Your own channels Your region, your province or onqc, as the people using it agree

Do this for each channel. The screenshots set #testing to yow; use your own label instead.

  1. Tap Channels in the bottom menu bar and open the channel.

  2. Tap ⋮ in the top right and choose Set Region Scope.

  3. If your label isn't listed, tap +, type it (for example yow) and tap the checkmark.

  4. If you added one, you'll see Region has been added! Tap your label to select it.

  5. The header now shows Region: yow. Only repeaters with that label on their region list pass this channel's messages on.

Scoped messages are a little shorter: the app allows fewer characters per message. On Public, the limit dropped from 137 to 127 characters in our testing.

docs.title: Bots and MeshMapper
docs.text:
Bots and MeshMapper use their region's label, such as ytr, so their messages stay in their own area.

  • Bots: on the bot's companion, set Default Region Scope to your region code, the same way as above. Set the channels it posts in to your region too.
  • MeshMapper: use your region code as the scope for its messages.

A labelled message only travels through repeaters that have its label, so check that the repeaters around you have been set up with it.

docs.title: Starter regions
docs.text:
Where MeshMapper has no zone yet, MeshCore Canada fills the gap with a starter region. Starter regions use real airport codes and work like any other region, but they're not MeshMapper zones, and they don't claim radio coverage. The Find your zone page draws them with dashed grey outlines. Check with local operators before relying on one.

Area Region Code from Prince Edward Island yyg Charlottetown Newfoundland yyt St. John's Labrador yyr Happy Valley–Goose Bay Yukon yxy Whitehorse Northwest Territories yzf Yellowknife Nunavut yfb Iqaluit

In the other provinces, these hubs fill the remaining gaps:

Province Starter regions BC ylw Kelowna, yxs Prince George, yxt Terrace, yxc Cranbrook AB ymm Fort McMurray, yqu Grande Prairie SK yxe Saskatoon, yqr Regina MB ybr Brandon, yth Thompson, yyq Churchill ON ysb Sudbury, yam Sault Ste. Marie, yts Timmins, yqk Kenora QC yvo Val-d’Or, yzv Sept-Îles, yvp Kuujjuaq NB yqm Moncton, yfc Fredericton NS yqi Yarmouth

Land that no region covers goes to the closest regional centre in its province: a MeshMapper region or one of the hubs above.

A repeater in Charlottetown has yyg, pe, can and na; one in Whitehorse has yxy, yt, can and na. Neither uses onqc. The setup tool gives the commands.

docs.title: Planning extensions
docs.text:
A gap right next to a MeshMapper region can use that region's code as a planning extension. For example, the Wingham-area point 43.8678, -81.2619 is in ykf, not Sudbury's ysb. Goderich is in yxu, and Kincardine in ylk.

Extensions are separate dashed areas on the map. They don't change MeshMapper's zones, and the Find your zone page says which kind of area your point is in. Like starter regions, they need local review and don't show measured radio coverage.

Starter regions and extensions are broad starting points, not a promise that distant towns can hear each other. MeshMapper's zones always come first: ask in MeshMapper to add or change a zone. To suggest a change to a starter region or an extension, send a community proposal.

The outlines follow Statistics Canada's province and territory boundaries. Labrador is census divisions 10 and 11; Newfoundland is the rest of the province.

docs.title: Build a 1 W solar repeater with the Ikoka Stick
Building a 1 W solar repeater — Ikoka Stick
docs.text:
By MrAlders0n (Ottawa) · Original guide: January 1, 2026

Build a solar-powered MeshCore repeater using a GOME Ikoka Stick, a junction box enclosure, and an epoxied solar panel.

Board: GOME Ikoka Stick (HW v0.4.0) Power: Waveshare Solar Power Manager (standard) Firmware: MeshCore

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
No warranty

This community build guide is provided without a warranty. Check continuity and polarity with a multimeter before applying power. Disconnect solar, battery, and USB power before soldering or changing wiring.

When to use a 1 W repeater

1 W repeaters are useful for backbone links and locations struggling to connect to the mesh. They are not needed at every site; coordinate with your local community.

Antenna required

Attach a LoRa antenna before powering the Ikoka Stick. Transmitting without an antenna can permanently damage the radio. Use the MeshCore power setting for your exact Ikoka radio module; a 1 W output rating is not an instruction to set TX power to 30 dBm.

docs.title: Parts list
docs.text:
Prices are from the original guide dated January 1, 2026, not current quotes. All amounts are in Canadian dollars; check availability, shipping, and taxes before ordering.

# Part Qty Price Source 1 GOME Ikoka Stick (HW v0.4.0) 1 $55 GitHub (group buy) 2 Waveshare Solar Power Manager (standard) 1 $15 Waveshare 3 IP65 Junction Box, 220x170x110mm, Gray 1 $30 AliExpress 4 Solar panel, 10W/18V, 250x340mm 1 $35 Amazon 5 3P1S 18650 battery pack (or 4P1S) 1 $25-35 MP&W Supply 6 Battery protection board (high/low voltage cutoff) 1 $8 Space Hedgehog 7 890-960MHz 4-cavity bandpass filter, 50W (recommended) 1 $65 Alibaba 8 10-15cm SMA right angle to N-Type female O-ring nut cable 1 $6 AliExpress 9 7.5cm SMA Male 90° to SMA Male 90° cable 1 $7 AliExpress 10 0.5ft USB-A to USB-C right angle cable 1 $7 Amazon 11 M3x35 spacers 4 12 M3x5 screws 8 13 Gorilla Epoxy Syringe, 25ml 1 $15 Home Depot 14 Waterproof vent plug (breather valve) 1 $2 AliExpress 15 Outdoor silicone caulk (clear) 1 $10 Any hardware store 16 Adafruit INA3221 (optional) 1 $15-20 DigiKey

Estimated total cost: ~$280-290 without the INA3221, ~$300-310 with it. This does not include the antenna, 3D-printed parts, or mounting hardware (M3 spacers/screws).

Alternative filter option (minimal): Callboost 915MHz cavity filter, 26M BW, $82. AliExpress

docs.title: Antenna
docs.text:
An antenna is not included in this parts list as selection will vary by deployment. It is highly recommended to use a higher dBi antenna such as a 6-8 dBi or higher with 1W builds. We have found that the Ikoka Stick does not pair well with the Alfa 5.8 dBi antenna for some reason, with several folks in Ottawa observing noticeably worse signal quality when using them together. This is not a definitive statement, just a pattern observed across multiple deployments.

For recommended antenna options, see the GOME Repeater Omni Antennas page.

docs.title: Tools required
docs.text: Tool Notes Soldering iron Fine tip recommended for I2C wiring Solder + flux Multimeter For continuity and voltage checks Step drill bit For drilling clean holes in the junction box Jigsaw or rotary tool For cutting the solar panel opening 1/8" drill bit For opening up mounting holes Pencil For marking the cutout Clamps + flat piece of wood For clamping solar panel during epoxy cure Wire strippers

docs.title: Printed parts and downloads
docs.text:
Before starting assembly, you will need the following 3D-printed parts. Both are available for download below:

  • Mounting plate for the junction box (holds the filter, Ikoka, and Waveshare board)

  • 3P1S 18650 battery holder (or sized to match your chosen battery configuration)

  • Mounting plate + 3P1S 18650 battery holder (combined .3mf)

  • Mounting plate (.stl)
  • 3P1S 18650 battery holder (.stl)

docs.title: Assembly steps
docs.text: Keep the solar panel, battery, and USB disconnected while cutting, soldering, or changing wiring.

docs.title: Enclosure Preparation
docs.text:
1. Flip the solar panel face-down. On the back, locate the black junction box where the red and black power wires exit. Measure this junction box with calipers or a ruler.

  2. On the front face of the gray junction box, use a pencil to trace a rectangle matching the solar panel junction box dimensions. Center it near the top of the panel.

  3. Using a step drill bit, drill a large starter hole in the center of the traced rectangle.

  4. Using a jigsaw or rotary tool, cut along the traced lines to remove the rectangular section. Clean up any rough edges.

docs.title: Mounting the Solar Panel
docs.text:
1. Mix a batch of Gorilla Epoxy and apply it generously across the entire front face of the junction box, covering the area where the solar panel will sit.

  2. Route the solar panel's power cable through the rectangular cutout from the outside into the box.

  3. Press the solar panel onto the epoxied face of the junction box. Place a flat piece of wood across the front of the panel and use clamps on all four corners to apply even pressure. Be careful not to over-tighten, as this can crack the panel. Alternatively, lay the assembly flat on the ground with weights on the back of the box.

  4. Allow the epoxy to fully cure according to the manufacturer's instructions before removing the clamps.

  5. Using clear outdoor silicone caulk, apply a bead around all four edges where the solar panel meets the junction box. Smooth the caulk to create a weatherproof seal.

docs.title: Mounting Plate and Filter
docs.text:
1. Attach the four M3x35 spacers to the corners of the junction box mounting plate. You may need to use a 1/8" drill bit to open the holes slightly to fit M3 screws through the plate. Use the 3D-printed mount plate as a reference for hole placement.

  2. Mount the RF bandpass filter to the mounting plate, positioning it roughly in the center.

  3. Connect the N-Type to SMA cable to the filter's output port. This cable will pass through the box wall to the external antenna.

  4. Determine where the N-Type connector should exit the junction box. Using a step drill bit, drill the hole, stepping up one size at a time and test-fitting after each step until the connector fits snugly.

  5. Feed the N-Type connector through the box wall from the inside out and tighten the O-ring nut to secure it.

  6. On the bottom of the junction box, drill a hole for the waterproof vent plug using the step drill bit.

  7. Install the vent plug and tighten it.

docs.title: Filter and Radio Preparation
docs.text:
1. Connect the SMA-to-SMA cable to the filter's input port. Finger-tighten for now.

  2. Waveshare Solar Power Manager prep (standard model): On the back of the board, solder a wire across the BOOT button pads to short it permanently. Without this modification, the board won't resume power output after a power loss, so your repeater would stay offline until you physically press the button.

docs.title: Component Mounting
docs.text:
1. Outside the box (for easier access), mount the Ikoka Stick and the Waveshare Solar Power Manager to the 3D-printed mounting plate. If using the optional INA3221, mount it as well.

  2. (Optional, Adafruit INA3221) Using a soldering iron, carefully remove the Ikoka Stick's OLED display header pins. Work slowly and gently to avoid damaging nearby components.

  3. (Optional, Adafruit INA3221) Solder the INA3221 to the Ikoka's I2C bus using the display header pads. See the INA3221 Wiring section below for the pin connections.

  4. Install the mounting plate assembly into the junction box and secure it with M3x5 screws into the M3x35 spacers.

docs.title: Battery Installation
docs.text:
1. Attach the 3D-printed battery holder to the inside front of the case, below where the solar panel wires enter. Use double-sided tape or epoxy to secure it.

  2. If your 18650 battery pack does not have a built-in PCM (protection circuit module), wire the battery protection board between the battery and the Waveshare. Follow the polarity markings carefully.

docs.title: Power Wiring
docs.text:
1. (Optional, Adafruit INA3221) Solar wiring: Connect the solar panel positive wire to INA3221 CH3+. Connect CH3- to the Waveshare solar input positive. Connect the solar panel negative wire directly to the Waveshare solar input negative.

  2. (Optional, Adafruit INA3221) Battery wiring: Connect the battery (or the PCM) positive wire to INA3221 CH1+. Connect CH1- to the positive pin on the Waveshare battery JST PH2.0 connector. Connect the battery negative wire directly to the negative pin on the JST PH2.0 connector. Plug the connector into the Waveshare board.

    Note: If you are not using the INA3221, wire the solar panel and battery directly to the Waveshare board's solar and battery inputs.

docs.title: Final Connections
docs.text:
1. Connect the SMA cable from the filter's input to the Ikoka Stick's SMA connector. Tighten both ends firmly with a wrench or pliers. A loose RF connection will cause signal loss.

  2. Run the USB-A to USB-C cable from the Waveshare Solar Power Manager's USB output to the Ikoka Stick's USB-C input.

    If using the Adafruit INA3221, your completed assembly should look similar to this:

    Without the INA3221:

    Full interior view with INA3221, battery pack, and all wiring complete:

docs.title: INA3221 wiring (optional)
docs.text:
The Adafruit INA3221 connects to the Ikoka Stick via I2C using the OLED display header pads. Remove the display header pins and solder wires directly to the pads.

I2C connection (Ikoka display header to INA3221):

Ikoka Display Header INA3221 Pin Wire Pin 1 - GND GND Ground Pin 2 - VCC (3.3V) VCC Power Pin 3 - SCL SCL Clock Pin 4 - SDA SDA Data

INA3221 channel assignments:

Channel Connected To Purpose CH1 Battery Monitor battery voltage and current draw CH2 (unused) Available for future use CH3 Solar Monitor solar input voltage and charging current

Note: VCC on the INA3221 is the board power pin (3.3V from the Ikoka). VIN1/VIN2/VIN3 are the measurement channel inputs, not the power pin.

docs.title: Firmware build flags
docs.text:
MeshCore defaults to address 0x42; the Adafruit INA3221 uses 0x40. Keep the inherited board flags and add the sensor settings to the 30 dBm repeater environment:

[env:ikoka_stick_nrf_30dbm_repeater]
build_flags =
  ${ikoka_stick_nrf_repeater.build_flags}
  ${ikoka_stick_nrf_e22_30dbm.build_flags}
  -D TELEM_INA3221_ADDRESS=0x40
  -UENV_INCLUDE_INA219
  -D TELEM_INA3221_SHUNT_VALUE=0.05

The address and INA219 flags are from the original guide: they select 0x40 and disable the conflicting INA219 driver. The shunt-value flag matches the Adafruit board's 0.05 Ω resistors so current readings use the correct scale. See Adafruit's pinout and MeshCore's sensor defaults.

docs.title: Test it on the bench
docs.text: Check polarity and continuity with a multimeter before you connect the battery. Then flash and configure the repeater, check that it comes back on by itself after you unplug the battery, and that a nearby companion hears its advert. The Waveshare manual has the power manager's limits.

docs.title: Recovery if it doesn't start
docs.text:
Disconnect power and recheck the wiring and the BOOT-button bridge. Stop using any battery that's hot, swollen or damaged.

docs.title: Build a 300 mW solar repeater
docs.text:
By MrAlders0n (Ottawa) · Original guide: January 1, 2026

A solar-powered MeshCore repeater in the RAK Unify Box enclosure. Follow each step carefully for a reliable, weatherproof build.

No warranty

This community build guide is provided without a warranty. Test everything with a multimeter before powering anything on. Questions? Ask MrAlders0n on the Discord.

docs.title: Parts list
docs.text:
Prices are from the original guide, dated May 2026, in Canadian dollars. Check current prices and shipping before ordering.

Item Product Cost (CAD) Link Enclosure WisMesh Unify Enclosure 910422 $72.50 AliExpress LoRa board RAK WisBlock RAK19003/RAK4631 (Type 6) $36.38 AliExpress Antenna ALFA AOA-915-5ACM $34.99 Amazon Antenna coax cable N female to IPX $6.79 AliExpress Battery 3000 mAh Li-ion, Makerfocus (pack of 4, Micro JST 2.0), ships from China $34.10 Makerfocus Battery protection ^ Li-ion PCM, Space Hedgehog $6.00 Space Hedgehog Vent Waterproof vent plug (M12×1.5-10) $6.12 AliExpress

^ The Makerfocus flat battery already includes a PCM; the extra PCM is an added safety measure. With unprotected batteries (such as 18650 button tops), you need a PCM.

Approximate total: $180 CAD

Using a different flat Li-ion battery

A battery with a different connector works too, but you need to change its connector to a Micro JST 2.0 and confirm the polarity (see the assembly steps). Example of a local battery with a Molex Picoblade 1.25 connector: Space Hedgehog. Example of a JST 2.0 connector: Adafruit.

docs.title: Assembly steps
docs.text:
Antennas before power

Always attach a LoRa antenna and the Bluetooth antenna to the RAK board before powering it on. Powering it without antennas can permanently damage the board.

  1. Unbox all the components and set them aside. Keep track of the small screws and fittings: they're easy to lose.
  2. Mount the RAK backplate into the box with the four provided screws.
  3. Drill two holes: one for the N-type antenna mount and one for the drain plug.
    • Use a step drill bit for clean holes.
    • To find the top of the box, flip it onto its back. The mount hole marked "1" is the top.
    • Drill slowly, one step at a time. Test-fit the N-type connector after each step until it fits snugly.
    • Do the same on the bottom of the box for the drain plug.
  4. Attach the N-type antenna mount and the drain plug.
  5. Connect the N-type antenna mount's cable to the LoRa IPEX connector on the RAK19003 board.
  6. Mount the Bluetooth antenna to the side of the box with the included double-sided tape.
  7. Connect the Bluetooth IPEX to the RAK19003 board.
  8. Connect an antenna to the N-type connector, then flash and configure the RAK with the repeater setup tool.

  9. Mount the RAK onto the backplate. It should look like this:

  10. Connect the JST PHR-2 cable to the RAK19003 battery plug, making sure the polarity is correct. Many JST cables are wired backwards.

  11. Connect the other end of this cable to the CHG side of the Li-ion PCM. This picture shows the Voltaic Enclosures PCM we used at first; the recommended PCM works the same way.

  12. Slide a piece of heat-shrink tubing, large enough to cover the PCM, over the cable before you connect the battery.

  13. Connect the battery's JST PHR-2 cable to the BATT side of the PCM, again making sure the polarity is correct.

  14. Heat-shrink the PCM so the whole board is covered.

  15. (Optional) Secure the PCM to the backplate with double-sided tape, or let it float freely inside the box.

  16. (Optional) Secure the battery to the backplate with double-sided tape or mounting hardware. It should look like this:

  17. Fit the rubber seal into the groove around the edge of the box's front plate.

  18. Connect the solar panel wire from the front plate to the RAK19003. Don't let the seal fall out of place while you do.
  19. Join the front and back plates and fasten them with the six screws. Tighten them securely to keep the seal weatherproof.
  20. Wrap the whole N-type connector and the exposed metal part of the Alfa antenna with self-fusing silicone tape, or use two layers of heat-shrink.

  21. Apply a bead of clear outdoor silicone caulk around the base of the N-type connector so water can't leak into the box.

  22. (Optional) Add a bead of silicone caulk along the top edge of the box seal, between the two plates, and around the base of the antenna for extra waterproofing.

docs.title: Test it on the bench
docs.text:
Before you mount it, check that it boots, keeps its settings after a reboot, and that a nearby companion hears its advert. If anything looks wrong, disconnect the battery and solar panel and recheck the polarity before trying again.
