docs.title: Set up a Station G3
docs.text:
By MrAlders0n (Ottawa) · October 19, 2026

Advanced

An advanced, high-power radio for experienced operators. New to repeaters? Start with Choose a repeater.

The Station G3 is a high-power LoRa base station with an external transmit amplifier (PA) and receive amplifier (LNA). Jumpers on the motherboard set how both behave. This page covers the G3-specific setup we use: the PA and LNA under firmware control, and about 30 dBm (1 W) out. Then finish it as a repeater or an observer.

Board: BQ Voyage / UnitEng Station G3 with the ESP32-S3 MCU board Firmware: MeshCore v1.17.1 or later, or the MQTT observer firmware Output: Power level 2 with set tx 16, about 30 dBm

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Antenna and power

Connect the antenna before applying power. Operating without an antenna can permanently damage the board. Power the G3 from a 9–19 V DC supply rated at 25 W or more through the barrel jack, or from a 15 V USB-C PD supply. Never exceed 19 V. The USB-C port on the MCU board is for data only and cannot power the G3.

Check your output power

The G3 can put out several watts. 30 dBm is 1 W at the antenna port, before cable loss and antenna gain. Antenna gain adds to the radiated power, so check current ISED rules against your full setup.

  • Flash a Station G3 build. Open the repeater setup tool and choose ESP32 with PSRAM when it asks what kind of board it is. When you reach the flasher, choose UnitEng/BQ Voyage Station G3 for a repeater, or Station G3 (ESP32) in the observer flasher for a repeater observer. Use a (2nd RF slot) build only if the LoRa card is in the second RF slot, which is not the default.
  • Have a data USB-C cable for the MCU board so you can use the console.

docs.title: How the power levels work
docs.text:
For MeshCore, we recommend removing the PA PL1 and LNA P jumpers so the firmware controls them. The PA then has four power levels, from level 1 (lowest) to level 4 (highest), set by the PA PL2 jumper and radio.fem.txgain:

PA PL2 jumper txgain off txgain on Removed Level 1 Level 3 Installed Level 2 Level 4

Level 4 needs a supply of at least 10 V. A new txgain value is saved straight away but only reaches the hardware at the start of the next transmit. Until then, get radio.fem.txgain can show the new value before the board has switched.

docs.title: Choose the TX setting
docs.text:
set tx sets the output of the SX1262 radio chip, which drives the PA. It is not the antenna output. The manufacturer's typical output at 915 MHz, in dBm:

set tx Level 1 Level 2 Level 3 Level 4 7 (default) 21.7 22.2 23.1 23.3 14 27.7 28.4 29.4 29.7 15 28.4 29.2 30.2 30.6 16 29.2 30.0 31.0 31.5 18 30.5 31.4 32.6 33.3 22 32.8 34.1 35.6 36.8

The bold values are the settings the manufacturer marks for US915 operation, all close to 30 dBm. The figures are typical, not a specification, so allow about ±2 dB. Do not copy set tx 22 from a generic guide: on a G3 that gives 33–37 dBm.

docs.title: 1. Set the jumpers
docs.text:
Power off the G3. The jumper block is beside the MCU header on the motherboard and is labelled PA PL1, PA PL2, LNA P, LNA S, and EEPROM.

Photo: BQ Voyage. PA PL1, PA PL2, and LNA P are installed here; for MeshCore, remove PA PL1 and LNA P.

Jumper Set to Why PA PL1 Removed The firmware sets it with radio.fem.txgain PA PL2 Installed txgain then switches between levels 2 and 4 LNA P Removed The firmware turns the LNA on for receive and off while transmitting LNA S Removed Reserved EEPROM Removed Reserved

LNA P works backwards from what you might expect: an installed jumper forces the LNA off.

The firmware cannot see the jumpers

If PA PL1 is still installed, set radio.fem.txgain off replies OK but the board stays on the higher level. Remove the jumper rather than relying on the command.

docs.title: 2. Set the amplifiers and TX power
docs.text:
Power the G3 back on, open the console over USB, and run:

set radio.fem.txgain off
set radio.fem.rxgain on
set tx 16

With PA PL2 installed, this is level 2 at about 30 dBm. For a different level, use the tables above.

radio.fem.rxgain controls the G3's external LNA. It is separate from radio.rxgain, which controls the radio chip's own receive gain.

docs.title: Check the setup
docs.text:
get radio.fem.txgain
get radio.fem.rxgain
get tx

You should see off, on, and 16.

docs.title: Troubleshooting and recovery
docs.text:
• Error: unsupported: the firmware is not a Station G3 build, or is older than MeshCore v1.17.1. Reflash with a Station G3 build.
  • Output stays high after txgain off: PA PL1 is still installed.
  • Weak reception: check that LNA P is removed and get radio.fem.rxgain shows on. Turning the LNA off can help at a site with a high noise floor.
  • Reboots when transmitting: the supply cannot keep up. Use a supply rated at 25 W or more, at least 10 V for level 4, or drop to a lower level.
  • To return to jumper-only control: power off and reinstall PA PL1 for levels 3 or 4. Only reinstall LNA P if you want the LNA off.

docs.title: Finish the setup
docs.text:
The G3-specific settings are done. Continue with the setup for this node's role:

  • Repeater: Set up a repeater to configure it and its regions.
  • Repeater observer: Set up a repeater observer to add Wi-Fi, your location code, and the MQTT presets.

docs.text:

  • MeshCore PR #3137: adds radio.fem.txgain and applies the level at the next transmit.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
What radio settings does MeshCore use in Canada?

Choose the Canada preset in the app. It sets the Canadian radio values and 3-byte paths; the separate USA preset uses the same radio values but leaves the path setting alone (preset update). The values are in the Canada defaults table.

Always check your community directory page in case a nearby mesh uses different settings.

What is 3-byte path hash mode?

MeshCore messages carry short repeater IDs along their path. MeshCore Canada recommends 3-byte IDs: bigger repeater networks get far more unique IDs than with the old 1-byte setting. In the MeshCore command line:

set path.hash.mode 2

Repeaters older than firmware 1.14 can't forward 2- or 3-byte paths. More in the upstream FAQ.

Do I need a ham radio licence?

MeshCore Canada can't give legal advice. Most Canadian MeshCore communities assume licence-exempt LoRa use in the right ISM band, but you're responsible for legal frequencies, power, antennas and duty cycle where you are.

If you operate as an amateur station or use non-standard equipment, check the current ISED rules before transmitting.

What range should I expect?

Range depends heavily on the antenna, height, terrain, obstructions, noise and line of sight. A handheld indoors may only cover a neighbourhood; a well-placed outdoor repeater with a clear view can cover much more.

When troubleshooting, compare against a nearby known-good node before assuming the firmware is at fault.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
What devices work with MeshCore?

Use devices listed in the MeshCore flasher or in a MeshCore Canada guide for the role you need. See Choose hardware.

For an observer, a supported Wi-Fi LoRa board can run as a repeater observer.

Can I use my Meshtastic device with MeshCore?

Sometimes, but it has to be flashed with MeshCore firmware and supported by the MeshCore build you choose. A device running Meshtastic won't join a MeshCore mesh.

Back up anything you care about before reflashing, and treat the first MeshCore flash as a new setup.

Which board should I buy first?

For a first companion, pick one that's listed in the MeshCore flasher and has community support near you: see Companions. For a fixed repeater or observer, stable power, a good antenna and remote access matter more than a screen.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
How do I join an existing mesh?
  1. Find your local page in the community directory.
  2. Choose the Canada preset unless the local page says otherwise.
  3. Check that paths are set to 3-byte.
  4. Reboot the device after changing radio settings.
  5. Send an advert and check whether nearby users can see you.
How do I start a new mesh in my area?

Use the Canada defaults unless you have a local reason to differ. Start with companions, then set up repeaters with the setup tool, which gives you every command to paste.

When you're ready, add your community to the directory with its region, status, contacts and any different settings.

Why does my observer show no packets?

A broker connection only proves the observer reached MQTT. It may still hear nothing if the radio preset or path setting is wrong, packet publishing is off, or no nearby nodes are active.

Use Check your observer and Troubleshooting to narrow it down.

Where can I ask another question?

See Get help: Discord and the forum are the quickest.

docs.title: Common tasks in the MeshCore app
docs.text:
Step-by-step guides for the most common things you'll do in the MeshCore mobile app.

  • Send your first message
  • Share your contact link
  • Import a contact link
  • Trace a path
  • Check heard repeats

docs.title: Send your first message
docs.text:
1. Open the app and connect to your companion.
  2. Open the Public channel, or your community's channel.
  3. Send a short hello and ask for a reply.

Heard X repeats under your message means a repeater picked it up. A reply means two-way messaging works.

docs.title: Share your contact link
docs.text:
1. Open the MeshCore app and connect to your node.

  2. Tap the Signal icon.

  3. Tap Advert → To Clipboard.

  4. Paste your contact link anywhere you want to share it.

docs.title: Import a contact link
docs.text:
1. Open the app and connect to your node.

  2. Tap the three dots.

  3. Tap Add Contact.

  4. Tap Import from Clipboard Link.

  5. After a few seconds you'll see "Success - contact has been imported".

  6. A second popup appears: "New Contact Discovered <NAME>".

  7. The contact is now added.

docs.title: One hop
docs.text:
1. Open the app and connect.

  2. Tap the three dots.

  3. Tap Tools.

  4. Tap Trace Path - Manual.

  5. Tap the plus button.

  6. Select a repeater and confirm.

  7. You'll see one repeater ID: that's a 1-hop trace.

  8. Tap Trace Path.

docs.title: Two or more hops
docs.text:
1. Follow steps 1 to 5 above.

  2. Select repeaters in order:

    • choose the forward path and confirm;
    • reopen the add menu and choose the return path;
    • or type the IDs yourself, for example d3, f3, d3.

  3. Confirm both the forward and return paths, then tap Trace.

  4. View the results.

docs.title: Check heard repeats
docs.text:
When you send a message, it travels to a nearby repeater, which repeats it. If your companion hears that repeat, it counts as a heard repeat. Your companion can miss a repeat, for example:

  • your message reaches the repeater, but the repeat doesn't make it back to you;

  • you're on a 1 W companion and the repeater is 0.3 W: you can reach it, but you may be too far away to hear its repeat.

  • Send a message in the Public channel.

  • When Heard X repeats shows under your message, press and hold the message.

  • Tap Heard Repeats.

  • You'll see every repeater your companion heard repeating that message.

  • Tap a repeater to see the path its repeat took back to you.

Notes:

  • A repeater close to you may show up as a direct hop.
  • You may also see a distant repeater. That happens when it hears your message shortly after another repeater and your companion hears both repeats.
  • Your companion must hear a repeater directly for it to appear in the list.

docs.text:

docs.title: What is MeshCore?
docs.text:
MeshCore is a repeater-driven long-range mesh network built on LoRa radios. The firmware you flash gives each device its job.

MeshCore project split, use the official links

Due to recent events in the MeshCore development team, the project has split. To stay on the official track, please only use:

  • Flashing tool and blog: meshcore.io
  • Source code: github.com/meshcore-dev/MeshCore
  • Discord (named "MeshCore.io"): discord.com/invite/fUfWevRXAg

Read more about the split: The Split, blog.meshcore.io.

docs.text:
• A companion sends and receives messages.
  • A repeater forwards traffic and extends coverage.
  • A room server keeps a shared room available.
  • An observer sends heard network data to Beacon.

docs.title: Change a repeater ID in 1-byte mode
docs.text:
Only for legacy 1-byte regions

Canada uses 3-byte path hashes by default. Continue only if your local region operator has confirmed this repeater must stay in 1-byte mode and approved the new ID.

docs.title: What this will change
docs.text: Changing the private key changes the node identity. It can break existing administration, contact, and tracking relationships. The old key is the only identity rollback path.

docs.title: Prerequisites and backup
docs.text:
1. Confirm with the local region operator that the repeater must remain in 1-byte mode and that a new ID is required.
  2. Connect to the repeater and record its current public key with get public.key.
  3. Over a trusted serial connection, or from the MeshCore app's Command Line after logging in to the repeater as admin, back up the current private key with get prv.key and store it as a secret in a secure location.
  4. Confirm the proposed 2–6 character ID is unused in the local region's coordination record.

Never post or transmit either private key through an issue, screenshot, public chat, or log. The saved old private key is the rollback path.

JavaScript is required for the live duplicate-ID check. You can also [open the live node directory](https://live.meshcore.ca/?tab=Nodes).

docs.title: Generate and apply the key
docs.text:
1. Open the MeshCore Key Generator.
  2. Enter the locally approved, unused 2–6 character ID and select Generate Key.
  3. Confirm the generated private key is a 64-character hexadecimal value.
  4. Copy it directly to the trusted repeater console without saving it in an ordinary note or chat.

  5. Run, replacing the placeholder with the generated value:

    set prv.key <PRIVATE-KEY>

  6. Reboot the repeater.

docs.title: Verify and restore
docs.text:
After reboot, run get public.key and confirm its prefix matches the locally approved ID. Recheck admin access, radio settings, region configuration, adverts, and local routing before returning the repeater to service.

If verification fails, restore the backed-up old private key with set prv.key <OLD-PRIVATE-KEY>, reboot, and confirm the original public key and access are restored.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: If admin access, the public-key prefix, adverts, region configuration, or routing is wrong, keep the repeater on the bench. Restore the backed-up old private key over the trusted serial connection, or from the MeshCore app's Command Line if you can still log in to the repeater as admin, reboot, and confirm the complete former state before returning it to service.

docs.title: Record the change
docs.text: Record the locally approved ID, operator approval, old/new public-key prefixes, verification, and rollback location without recording either private key in the public maintenance record.

docs.title: Verification limits
docs.text: This procedure has not been tested against current firmware. Have the local region operator review it before use.

docs.title: Update a repeater or room server over the air
Before you start
docs.text:
Bootloader first

Only do this if the repeater has the OTAFIX bootloader. The repeater setup tool walks through the bootloader update for nRF52 boards.

Android only: iOS not recommended

These steps are for Android. iOS technically works, but we've had several failed OTA updates from iOS. Until that changes, don't use an iOS device for OTA updates.

This only applies to nRF-based boards (for example the RAK4630, Heltec T114 and XIAO nRF52). We strongly recommend updating over USB instead.

OTA risks

An OTA update can fail even when the app says it worked, and then the repeater needs a USB re-flash. We had one fail in winter and had to wait until spring to reach the repeater. Proceed at your own risk.

Save the repeater's private key first, in case a failed update forces a USB re-flash: log in as admin, open Command Line and send get prv.key. Keep the reply in a password manager and never share it.

These steps summarise the official instructions on the MeshCore blog.

docs.title: 1. Download the firmware .zip
docs.text:
1. Open the MeshCore flasher and find your device.
  2. Select the Repeater or Room Server role, then the latest version.
  3. Click Download at the bottom right and choose the .zip file.

You can also download the .zip for your board (for example, the T114 repeater) from the MeshCore GitHub releases.

docs.title: 2. Log in and start OTA
docs.text:
1. In the MeshCore app, log in to the device with the admin password.

  2. Open the Command Line tab and send:

    start ota

  3. You should see a reply like:

    OK - mac: FF:AA:BB ...

Tip: a standalone device such as a T-Deck running Ripple can also send start ota.

docs.title: 3. Connect with your phone
docs.text: Install Nordic's nRF Device Firmware Update app from Google Play if you don't have it.

docs.title: DFU app settings
docs.text:
Tap the Settings icon and set:

  • Packet receipts notification: ON
  • Number of packets: 8
  • Request high MTU: OFF
  • Disable resume: ON
  • Prepare object delay: 0 ms
  • Force scanning: ON

docs.title: Start the update
docs.text:
1. Select the .zip file you downloaded.
  2. Select your device from the scan list.
  3. Press Start and wait for the update to finish.

docs.title: 4. Check it updated
docs.text:
1. Log out and log back in, with the app or a standalone device.
  2. Check the clock with clock. If it's wrong, send clock sync.
  3. Send ver to confirm the firmware version changed.

docs.title: Recovery if it fails
docs.text:
If the update stalls or fails, send this from your phone or a standalone device, then try again:

reboot

RAK4631 with the updated bootloader: the app will likely say the flash failed. Scan again: the device shows up with a generic name (such as AdaDFU or RAK4631_DFU). Select it and upload the update again.

Setting Canada default Radio preset Canada Raw radio values 910.525 MHz / 62.5 kHz / SF7 / CR5 Path hash mode 3-byte Command-line path setting set path.hash.mode 2

The MeshCore app now has separate Canada and USA presets. Both use the radio values above, but Canada also selects 3-byte paths. USA leaves the path-hash setting unchanged. You can still change that setting manually. See the September 9 preset update.

If your app or flasher still shows USA/Canada (Recommended), use it for the same radio values and set 3-byte paths separately. Update repeaters older than firmware 1.14 before relying on multi-byte paths; those older versions cannot forward them.

docs.title: MeshCore glossary
docs.text: Use your browser's Find command to jump to a term. Definitions are short; the linked guides explain how to use each setting or device.

docs.title: A-E
docs.text: Advert A MeshCore announcement packet that helps nearby nodes learn about a device and its path. Bandwidth A LoRa radio setting that affects how much radio spectrum a transmission uses. Use the value from your local settings or the setup tool. Broker A service that receives and distributes messages for Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT). City repeater A repeater that passes on messages with no label, so people nearby who haven't set a scope are still heard. Every repeater that isn't an edge repeater is a city repeater. See City or edge repeater. Coding rate (CR) A LoRa error-correction setting. Use the value from your local settings or the setup tool. Companion A personal MeshCore device used to send and receive messages. It often connects to an app and does not relay mesh traffic. Beacon MeshCore Canada's public tools for viewing observers, packets, nodes, and map data. Edge repeater A repeater that regularly hears repeaters in another region, for example one between Belleville and Kingston. It doesn't pass on messages with no label, so they don't spill into the next region. See City or edge repeater.

docs.title: F-M
docs.text: Firmware Software installed on a device. MeshCore firmware is built for a specific board and role. Industrial, scientific, and medical (ISM) band Radio spectrum used by many low-power devices. Legal use still depends on location, equipment, and operating conditions. JSON Web Token (JWT) A time-limited credential used by supported MeshCore Canada data services. Treat it as sensitive. Location code A short code that groups observer data by area. Some observer guides call this an IATA code because they use three-letter airport codes. LoRa The long-range, low-power radio modulation used by MeshCore devices. Mesh network A network in which supported devices can relay traffic instead of relying on one central radio. Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) A publish-and-subscribe protocol used by observers to send network data to public tools.

docs.title: N-R
docs.text: Node Any MeshCore device on the network. Observer A radio or host service that listens for MeshCore traffic and sends network data to public tools. Observing and repeating are separate functions; a node can do both when configured for it. Path hash mode The MeshCore setting that controls the size of identifiers in advert paths. Use the value from the current local or Canadian configuration. Preset A named group of radio settings. Region The area a repeater serves, named after the nearest airport code. A region list is the labels a repeater agrees to pass on. See Scopes and regions. Repeater A normally fixed MeshCore device that relays packets to extend network coverage. Repeater observer A repeater that also reports what it hears to live.meshcore.ca, so everyone can see how the mesh is doing. It needs Wi-Fi, so it needs an ESP32 board. See What a repeater observer is. Room server A MeshCore device that keeps a shared room available to companions. Its main job is hosting the room, not extending coverage.

docs.title: S-W
docs.text: Scope (region scope) A scope is a label on a message saying how far it should travel. You set a default on your companion, and a channel can have its own. See Scopes and regions. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) A measurement comparing a received signal with background noise. Spreading factor (SF) A LoRa setting that affects airtime, data rate, and reception. Use the value from your local settings or the setup tool. WebSocket A long-lived web connection. Some MQTT clients use WebSockets to reach a broker through normal web network paths.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
New to MeshCore? Most people start with a companion: a small radio that pairs with your phone so you can send messages.

Pick the device you're setting up:

  • Companion

    Send and receive messages. Goes with you, paired to your phone.

    Set up a companion

  • Repeater

    Extends coverage by relaying everyone's messages. Fixed, up high and always powered.

    Set up a repeater

  • Room server

    Hosts a shared chat room that keeps recent messages. Fixed and always powered.

    Set up a room server

  • Observer

    Sends what it hears to the Beacon network maps. Fixed and always powered.

    Set up an observer

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Companions don't relay messages for others. Leave client repeat off on an established mesh unless your local community says otherwise.
  • Room servers can relay, but don't use them that way. Put up a separate repeater instead.
  • Standalone devices with a screen and keyboard, like the T-Deck, aren't recommended for a first device. Their firmware is still rough.

docs.title: Radio settings
docs.text:
Use your local community's settings from the community directory. If none are listed, use the Canada defaults.

Not sure what you need? Ask the community before buying hardware.

docs.title: Set up a companion
docs.text: A companion is your personal MeshCore radio. It pairs with the MeshCore app on your phone so you can send and receive messages. It doesn't relay messages for anyone else. Setup takes about 20 to 30 minutes.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A supported device. See the recommended companions, and check that the MeshCore flasher lists your exact board.
  • A USB cable that carries data. Charge-only cables won't work.
  • Chrome or Edge on a computer. The flasher needs Web Serial. Some boards also need a USB serial driver.
  • The MeshCore app on your phone, version 1.43 or newer.

docs.title: Used this device before? Back it up first
docs.text:
Erase Flash deletes the device's stored data

That includes its identity (private key), name, contacts, channels and radio settings. An erased identity can't be recovered unless you backed it up.

  1. Connect with the app that manages it now.
  2. Note its name, radio settings and anything else you'd need to set again.
  3. Export its private key with your app's backup option. Keep it secret: never post it in a screenshot, chat or issue.
  4. Export contacts and channels if your app offers it.

If you can't back up something you need, stop before Erase Flash and ask for help.

docs.title: 1. Flash the firmware
docs.text:
1. Connect the device to your computer by USB.
  2. Open the MeshCore flasher and select your exact board.
  3. Select Companion Radio (Bluetooth) and the firmware version for that board.
  4. Follow the flasher's connection steps. Use Enter DFU Mode only if your board asks for it.
  5. New device or deliberate reset? Back up first, then click Erase Flash only if your board's instructions require it. For an update, leave erase off.
  6. Click Flash and wait for the completion message before unplugging.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text: When it's done, the board restarts as a companion and the app can find it.

docs.title: Recovery if flashing fails
docs.text: Don't keep erasing. Leave the device connected, refresh the flasher, put the board back in DFU mode, select the same board and companion firmware, and try Flash again. If the board no longer shows up, ask for help before trying anything else.

docs.title: 2. Name it and set the radio
docs.text:
1. Open the MeshCore app and pair with your companion.
  2. Give it a name that doesn't reveal where you live.
  3. Check the community directory for your area's settings. If none are listed, choose Canada (910.525 MHz / 62.5 kHz / SF7 / CR5) and confirm 3-byte paths.
  4. Save. The device restarts; reconnect when it's back.

Use Canada unless your community lists different settings. If Canada isn't in your app, follow the older-preset instructions.

docs.title: 3. Set your default scope
docs.text:
Set your default scope now

Repeaters set up with the meshcore.ca setup tool pass messages on by scope. Edge repeaters don't pass on messages that have no scope, so without a default scope your messages may not reach beyond your own area.

  • Ontario or Québec: use onqc.
  • Elsewhere: use your province's code, such as ns or bc, unless your community has agreed on something else.

docs.title: Set it in the MeshCore app
docs.text:
The screenshots use onqc; type your own scope if you're elsewhere.

  1. Connect your companion to the MeshCore app and tap the settings cog in the top right.

  2. Scroll down to Network Settings and tap Default Region Scope.

  3. If your scope is not listed, tap Add Region, or the + at the top right.

  4. Type your scope, all lowercase, and tap the checkmark in the top right.

  5. Tap your scope to select it.

  6. Default Region Scope now shows your scope. Tap the checkmark in the top right. It spins while saving, then Settings Saved! pops up.

  7. Find your city code on the Find your zone page.

  8. Ontario and Québec: also use onqc on the Public channel, and your city scope (such as yow) on test channels. Open the channel, tap ⋮ and choose Set Region Scope.
  9. Leave can and na for future use.
  10. Running a bot or MeshMapper? Follow the bot and MeshMapper instructions.

How repeaters work explains scopes with examples. Scopes don't change your radio settings.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Send a message in the Public channel.
  2. Heard X Repeats means a repeater picked it up. A plain Sent doesn't mean your settings are wrong: you may be out of range. Move somewhere with known coverage or ask your community to help test.
  3. Reboot the companion and check that its name and settings stuck.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Find your community and say hello.
  • Learn the app with the MeshCore how-to guides.
  • Nobody hears you? Get help.

docs.title: Get help
docs.text:
The quickest way to get help is to ask the community:

Ask on Discord Ask on the forum

Never post passwords, private keys, precise locations or unredacted command output.

docs.title: What to include
docs.text:
• your device type and model;
  • the page and step where you got stuck;
  • what you expected, and what happened instead;
  • the radio preset you're using (Canada or your community's);
  • any error text, with sensitive values removed.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text:
What's wrong? Try this Not sure which device you need Get started Nobody hears your advert Recheck the radio settings and the Test it step on your setup page You need local settings or someone to test with Find a community An observer is missing or quiet Observer troubleshooting A general MeshCore question MeshCore FAQ A page here is wrong or missing something Share an idea

Change one thing at a time, then test again. It makes the result much easier to understand.

docs.title: Stop and ask before you retry if
docs.text:
• the next step would erase data you haven't backed up;
  • the hardware is hot, damaged, wet or wired unexpectedly;
  • you'd lose your only way to reach a remote node;
  • a local operator says your settings conflict with the mesh.

docs.title: Set up a room server
docs.text: A room server hosts a shared chat room on the mesh. People log in with a guest password and can catch up on messages they missed. It isn't a repeater: put up a separate repeater for coverage.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A supported device that the MeshCore flasher offers Room Server firmware for.
  • A USB cable that carries data. Charge-only cables won't work.
  • Chrome or Edge on a computer. The flasher needs Web Serial.
  • Someone to look after it. Decide who keeps the admin password and can reach the device by USB if it needs fixing.

docs.title: Used this device before? Back it up first
docs.text:
Erase Flash deletes stored room-server data

That includes its identity (private key), room messages, guest and admin access, name and radio settings.

  1. Note its name, radio settings and access settings.
  2. Save its private key with a supported tool. Keep it secret.
  3. Keep passwords in a password manager, never in screenshots, issues or chat.

If you can't back up something you need, stop before Erase Flash and ask for help.

docs.title: 1. Flash the firmware
docs.text:
1. Connect the device to your computer by USB.
  2. Open the MeshCore flasher and select your exact board.
  3. Select Room Server and the firmware version for that board.
  4. Follow the flasher's connection steps. Use Enter DFU Mode only if your board asks for it.
  5. New device or deliberate reset? Back up first, then click Erase Flash only if your board's instructions require it. For an update, leave erase off.
  6. Click Flash and wait for the completion message before unplugging.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text: The device restarts as a room server, and Configure via USB in the flasher can connect to it.

docs.title: Recovery if flashing fails
docs.text: Don't keep erasing. Leave the device connected, refresh the flasher, put the board back in DFU mode, select the same board and Room Server firmware, and try Flash again. If the board no longer shows up, ask for help before trying anything else.

docs.title: 2. Name it and set passwords and radio
docs.text:
1. In the flasher, click Configure via USB and connect to the device.
  2. Give it a name that doesn't reveal a private location.
  3. Set a guest password (shared with people who should join the room) and a different admin password (kept private). Store both in a password manager.
  4. Check the community directory for your area's settings. If none are listed, choose Canada (910.525 MHz / 62.5 kHz / SF7 / CR5) and 3-byte paths (set path.hash.mode 2).
  5. Save and reboot.

Use Canada unless your community lists different settings. If Canada isn't offered, follow the older-preset instructions.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
Do this on the bench before you put it anywhere hard to reach.

  1. Send an advert from the room server.
  2. Check that a nearby companion finds it.
  3. Log in from the companion with the guest password.
  4. Reboot it and check that its name, passwords and radio settings stuck.

If anything fails, keep it plugged in by USB, flash it again and repeat the test.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Tell your local community the room exists and how to get the guest password.
  • Ask someone nearby to test it from their own companion.
  • Something not working? Get help.

docs.title: L’outil de configuration
docs.text:
L’outil de configuration ne demande ni ne conserve jamais votre mot de passe administrateur ni votre mot de passe Wi-Fi. Là où une commande en exige un, elle affiche un espace réservé que vous remplissez vous-même.

  • Partager et reprendre. Le lien de l’outil (Copier un lien vers ces réponses, qui est aussi l’adresse dans votre navigateur) contient vos réponses non secrètes, comme le nom du répéteur, sa région, le lieu choisi (une ville ou une adresse) et les coordonnées de l’épingle que vous avez placée sur la carte, pour que vous puissiez partager ou reprendre une configuration. Il ne contient jamais de mots de passe, de renseignements Wi-Fi ni de réponse region collée. Les liens peuvent apparaître dans l’historique du navigateur et les journaux du serveur : ne partagez pas un lien qui contient un emplacement privé.
  • Emplacement sur la carte. L’outil affiche une carte avec une épingle, que vous pouvez déplacer. Les commandes règlent l’emplacement du répéteur à l’épingle, et tout le monde peut voir cet endroit sur les cartes publiques. La plupart des gens choisissent un endroit à une rue ou deux du répéteur. Si vous cochez Désactiver l’emplacement, l’outil retire ces commandes de la liste, et le lieu et l’épingle restent aussi hors du lien.
  • Changer de langue. Pour ne pas vous faire recommencer, l’outil garde vos coches, la version du micrologiciel et les réponses collées dans cet onglet du navigateur, seulement le temps du changement. L’autre page les utilise une seule fois, puis les supprime. Passé 10 minutes, ils sont ignorés, et ils disparaissent à la fermeture de l’onglet.
  • Fichiers de régions. MeshMapper n’est pas contacté, sauf si vous cliquez sur un lien qui y mène. L’outil de configuration, Comprendre les répéteurs et Trouver votre zone lisent les fichiers de régions publiés sur ce site.

docs.title: Données enregistrées sur votre appareil
docs.text:
La page Trouver votre zone met dans son adresse Web (URL) seulement le code de zone et la province que vous avez choisis, par exemple ?tag=ytr&province=on, pour que vous puissiez partager ou recharger la page. Elle n’y met jamais de ville, d’adresse civique ni de coordonnées, et le changement de langue ne transmet rien. Les liens peuvent apparaître dans l’historique du navigateur et les journaux du serveur.

Les brouillons d’idées et le dernier code de région Beacon choisi dans l’outil de vérification sont enregistrés uniquement dans votre navigateur lorsque vous utilisez ces fonctions. Les clés publiques des répéteurs, les mots de passe, les clés privées, les jetons antipourriel et les recherches d’emplacement n’y sont pas enregistrés.

Les totaux de l’en-tête sont mis en cache pendant cinq minutes dans l’onglet courant. La ville recherchée dans le répertoire apparaît dans l’URL pour partager ou retrouver les résultats.

Vous pouvez effacer les données enregistrées par ce site dans les paramètres de votre navigateur. Le formulaire d’idée offre aussi l’action Effacer le brouillon enregistré.

L’ancien éditeur de régions peut télécharger les brouillons conservés dans ce navigateur. Le téléchargement ne les envoie ni ne les supprime; ces brouillons ne sont pas des limites approuvées dans MeshMapper.

docs.title: Données des observateurs et vie privée
docs.text:
Considérez le trafic radio MeshCore comme public

Le trafic MeshCore est destiné à un usage partagé, et les réseaux peuvent utiliser des préréglages ou des fréquences différents. Considérez tous les canaux qui utilisent une clé partagée, et les canaux privés aussi, comme non sécurisés : tout nœud qui utilise les mêmes réglages peut être capté par les observateurs de ce réseau. Le trafic relayé par MQTT doit être considéré comme public. N’envoyez pas de noms, d’emplacements, de notes ou d’autres renseignements personnels que vous ne voudriez pas voir conservés et affichés publiquement. Partez du principe que même un canal privé pourrait être recueilli et déchiffré par quelqu’un qui en a les moyens et le savoir-faire.

docs.title: Ce que nous recueillons
docs.text:
Les serveurs MQTT de MeshCore Canada reçoivent des données de paquets des observateurs qui captent les paquets MeshCore et relaient la télémétrie.

Les observateurs écoutent tout le trafic MeshCore qu’ils peuvent capter avec leurs réglages. Si un observateur capte un paquet et que la publication des paquets est activée, ce paquet peut être envoyé aux serveurs de MeshCore Canada.

docs.title: Où vont les données
docs.text:
Étape Ce qui se passe Trafic radio Les nœuds envoient des paquets MeshCore sur les fréquences et réglages de leur réseau local. Captation par l’observateur Les observateurs écoutent tout le trafic qu’ils peuvent capter avec leurs réglages. Publication MQTT Les observateurs publient les données des paquets sur les serveurs de MeshCore Canada. Stockage et affichage Les données sont conservées sur l’infrastructure de MeshCore Canada et peuvent être affichées par Beacon et d’autres sites publics exploités par MeshCore Canada ou des exploitants approuvés.

Aucune durée de conservation n’a encore été publiée : ne présumez pas que les données sont supprimées après un certain temps.
